power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

Integrating evolutionary science, neuroscience, and cognitive science, adaptive moral theory (AMT) offers a consilient account of our evolved moral sense.

It proposes two functionally distinct moral systems: the foundational mammalian CARE system and the phylogenetically newer duty network, advancing a working definition of morality centered on the well-being of other living entities.

AMT also reconceptualizes the emotion/reason debate and provides a new account of the relationship between consequentialism and deontology; it also challenges cooperation-centered evolutionary accounts, naturalizes situation ethics, and introduces a taxonomy of eight moral frames that offers a different lens on sacrificial dilemmas.
Nature, red in tooth and claw, but also warm in heart and paw, has built within the human brain the capacity to feel emotions (from movere: to move).
When they're working adaptively, they impel us to move, to act.
But it has also built within us a capacity to reason (from reri: to reckon), which provides us with more behavioral options.
This dichotomy was recognized by ancient thinkers across civilizations, long before the Greeks formalized it as a conflict between the irrational and rational parts of the soul.
Since then, philosophers have debated whether our moral sense arises from emotion, reason, or some interaction of the two.

This was all a matter of philosophy until the sciences started shining their light on these questions -beginning with Darwin, but particularly in the 20th century, when we began locating emotion and cognition in the brain.

In recent decades, with advances in evolutionary theory, neuroimaging, and the psychological and cognitive sciences, the debate has continued (e.g., Greene et al., 2001; Greene, 2008 Greene, , 2013;; Haidt, 2001).

text.text: Moral philosophy has also wrestled with another tension, though not for nearly as long.
From Kant to Rawls and Bentham to Singer, the field has struggled with an apparent incompatibility between two of its three central theories: consequentialism and deontology.
Crudely, what 3 makes an act or decision right can be answered in terms of its outcomes (consequentialism) or the duties it upholds or violates (deontology).
While the reasons for this tension are overdetermined, one, perhaps, is the constraining nature of moral philosophy's inherited constructs and disciplinary boundaries.

4   Integrating insights from neuroscience, cognitive science, and the evolutionary sciences with 5 new theoretical frameworks for understanding the underlying structure of our moral sense (and morality more broadly), adaptive moral theory (AMT) reinterprets these longstanding tensions.
It provides a new account of the relationship between consequentialism and deontology and argues that the emotion/reason binary, real as it is, obscures a clearer understanding of morality.

Challenging recent evolutionary approaches that frame morality primarily as a solution to the problems of cooperation and conflict (Curry, 2016; Wilkinson et al., 2024; Greene, 2013), AMT I've left out a treatment of virtue ethics due to space constraints, though I believe AMT can account for it, as well.

text.text: Our earliest moral behaviors were regulated entirely by the CARE system, which guided behaviors like parenting, helping, and resource sharing.

CARE is the evolutionary and affective foundation, but the other part of what constitutes our moral sense is what adaptive moral theory calls the duty network (hereafter, also DN or Duty). 7 The DN is akin to what the dominant traditions of normative ethics treat as the core of morality -rules, duties, principles.

text.text: Kant's rationalism, in fact, holds that only acts from duty have genuine moral worth.
AMT disagrees.
CARE, too, is part of our morality; thus, action springing from it can carry genuine moral worth.
For AMT, CARE is foundational, but both the CARE system and the duty network are irreducible and fundamental to morality.
The duty network is a proposed neural network; thus, all claims about its instantiation are conjectural.
And while termed 'Duty,' it is the seat of far more: moral rules, social contracts, fairness principles, reciprocal agreements, codes, obligations, religious tenets, commitments, and so on.
Although these rules may have originally evolved to protect well-being through principles of care and non-harm, the network is strictly rule-based and, importantly, can conflict with care.

As we move to more abstract or large-scale moral problems (e.g., trolley problems and other sacrificial dilemmas), our moral decision-making becomes more complex; for these, AMT introduces eight moral frames.
Finally, AMT provides a naturalistic foundation for situation ethics -the intuitive but philosophically neglected view that privileges context.

Which great philosopher, so far, has been married?
Heraclitus, Plato, Descartes, Spinoza, Leibniz, Kant, Schopenhauer -were not; indeed it is impossible to even think about them as married.

A married philosopher belongs to comedy, that is my proposition…" -Nietzsche, On the Genealogy of Morals (1887) This sentimentalist lineage (moral judgment grounded in emotion or passion rather than pure reason) traces back at least to 6 Hume and Smith.

text.text: Why "adaptive moral theory" and not "evolutionary ethics" (an established field)?
EE is too narrow.
In addition to evolutionary 7 theory, AMT integrates neuroscience and cognitive science, proposing a different account of morality's origin and function.
'Adaptive' is also more apt: our moral sense evolved and is adaptive; our moral networks are adaptive; moral rules adapt to context.

While AMT is an explanatory metatheory and not a normative ethical framework, the term "adaptive ethics" might be useful in the future, as AMT's implications are potentially normative and prescriptive.

text.text: Does moral worth -and morality itself -rest on compassion or duty, emotion or reason?
The answer is surely mu -these questions are not answerable in their form.

Hume not 8 only saw this, he also located morality's foundation naturalistically: "These arguments on each side . . . are so plausible, that I am apt to suspect . . . that reason and sentiment concur in almost all moral determinations and conclusions. . .
[But it] depends on some internal sense or feeling, which nature has made universal in the whole species" (1777/1975, 1.9).
But the emotion/reason binary Hume inherited shrouds our view of the moral landscape.
To see more clearly, we need to step outside the bounds of philosophy.
Paul MacLean's (1973) triune brain theory posited that the brain evolved in stages: first the reptilian brain (reflexes), then the limbic system (emotions), then the neocortex (reason).

text.text: These independent biological, developmental, and behavioral lines of evidence are consistent with -and lend support to -AMT's claim that the CARE system is the foundational basis of morality.

Following affective neuroscientist Jaak Panksepp's identification of CARE as one of seven primary emotional systems (which he capitalized), AMT recognizes this primal system of care, empathy, and nurturance as foundational.
This aligns with common-sense intuitions, as well as the ethics-of-care tradition: that care for the well-being of others is central to morality.
While CARE is capitalized here to build on Panksepp's pioneering work, AMT's CARE is broader than Panksepp's in both scope and neuroanatomy.

text.text: AMT proposes that symbolic and linguistic capacities compressed CARE's evolved responses into portable cognitive algorithms: principles and rules.
Through repeated engagement, these algorithms gradually shaped neural pathways into what AMT calls the duty network.
Just as CARE is a functional, affective-motivational system not reducible to emotion, the duty network is a functional rule system not reducible to rationality.
The proposed DN is a neural network for representing, maintaining, and applying social rules -and for detecting their violation.
On AMT's account, well-studied capacities such as cheater detection (Cosmides & 13 Tooby, 1992) are instances of this broader violation-detection function.
text.formatted: On AMT's account, well-studied capacities such as cheater detection <ref type="bibr">(Cosmides & 13</ref> Tooby, 1992) are instances of this broader violation-detection function.

text.text: The duty network's core rules are CARE-derived.
Its sensitivity to violation may have 14 originated in protective responses to the mistreatment of oneself (proto-CARE) and of others (CARE).
Despite its origins, the duty network tracks transgression rather than care.
It can therefore take up any rule represented as socially binding, including culturally acquired rules that may conflict with its core rules.
(E.g., for some, a mandate for female genital mutilation can override the DN's core injunction against bodily injury.)

Like other large-scale brain networks (e.g., the default mode network, the salience network), the duty network likely comprises many connected areas working together, engaging flexibly depending on the novelty and complexity of the moral situation.

This is consistent with Boyd and Richerson's work on cultural rules as cognitive shortcuts (1985, 2005), and is supported by neuroplasticity research (Draganski et al., 2004; Woollett & Maguire, 2011); Dehaene's (2009) research showing how cultural inventions such as reading create specialized neural circuits; and Anderson's (2016) theory of neural reuse (repurposing existing neural circuits for new cognitive and behavioral functions).

text.text: With these group-level lenses, prosocial emotions, altruism, and moral norms can be understood as adaptations shaped by selection among groups, rather than solely as strategies serving individual genetic fitness.
The most influential recent evolutionary accounts, however, build on the dominant view in evolutionary theory -inclusive fitness and kin selection -and increasingly center on cooperation.

Evolutionary moral psychologist Oliver Scott Curry states that "morality is a collection of biological and cultural solutions to the problems of cooperation and conflict recurrent in human social life; and game theory reveals what those problems and solutions are" (Curry, 2016, p. 44).

text.text: His theory of Morality as Cooperation (MAC) identifies at least seven distinct types of cooperation: allocation of resources to kin, coordination to mutual advantage, social exchange, dominance, submission, division of disputed resources, and recognition of prior possession.
Similarly, Greene asserts that "morality is a set of psychological adaptations that allow otherwise selfish individuals to reap the benefits of cooperation" (2013, p. 23).
In contrast, I define morality as follows:
Morality is the realm of affairs involved in ensuring, benefitting, increasing, and sustaining the survival and well-being of other living entities.

Evolved adaptations such as the emotions and the mammalian CARE system, as well as higher-order cognitive rules (implicit and explicit), motivate, regulate, constrain, and govern behavioral efforts within this realm.
While the two theories -MAC and AMT -are not incompatible, they focus on different parts of the moral landscape.
AMT agrees that MAC's seven types of cooperation are part of the picture; they can be understood through CARE, the duty network, or their interaction.

But, while Curry acknowledges that moral motivation, values, and emotion are relevant to morality, he argues that "'care' -like 'altruism' -is a generic term that does not distinguish between forms of prosocial behavior with different ultimate and proximate roots" (Curry et al., 2019, p. 50).

text.text: 'Care' is generic.
But the CARE/Duty framework is not.
It can make those distinctions.

For example, kin care evolved via inclusive fitness -direct fitness through parental investment, indirect fitness through kin selection -proximately mediated by the CARE system, and, later, by the DN's filial obligation.
Reciprocal altruism is ultimately an exchange strategy among nonkin.
Its rules, such as promise-keeping and debt repayment, are proximately implemented by the duty network (with its origins in CARE).

Curry further explains that care is not related to any specific type of cooperation and therefore predicts that it will not constitute one of the seven corresponding moral domains: family values, group loyalty, reciprocity, heroism, deference, fairness, and property rights (Curry et al., 2019).

text.text: For AMT, CARE is not one of seven domains; it is one of morality's two fundamental systems -and it's the foundational one.
Each of our theories identifies a different organizing feature of morality.

For MAC, it's cooperation, so care is easy to write off; for AMT, it's care and concern for the well-being of others, mediated by the C/D framework, with cooperation among the norms the duty network codifies.

MAC's emphasis on cooperation and AMT's emphasis on care recall psychologist and ethicist Carol Gilligan's seminal challenge to moral psychologist Lawrence Kohlberg's theory of moral development, which placed reasoning about justice and rights at the highest stage, while treating care-based reasoning as less morally advanced.

In her book In a Different Voice (1982), Gilligan wrote: "The moral imperative that emerges repeatedly in interviews with women is an injunction to care, a responsibility to discern and alleviate the 'real and recognizable trouble' of this world.
For men, the moral imperative appears rather as an injunction to respect the rights of others and thus to protect from interference the rights to life and self-fulfillment" (p. 100).
Just as Gilligan challenged a framework that privileged rules and fairness and undervalued care, AMT challenges evolutionary approaches that privilege cooperation and undervalue care.
Not only is AMT a Kantian-Schopenhauerian synthesis, it is a Gilligan-Kohlberg synthesis.

text.text: In each case, these rules protect the well-being of persons.
The categories may not be exhaustive, and violations may involve more than one category.
(For example, whether the protection of relational bonds warrants a distinct category remains an open question.)
The prohibitive structure set forth is particularly relevant to the duty network's proposed role in rule-violation detection.
But CARE also gives rise to duties of beneficence -to aid, protect, and support others -which are left for future work.

These first principles -the duty to extend care (beneficence) and the duty to do no harm (nonmaleficence) -were codified in our earliest moral codes, from ancient Egyptian teachings like Ma'at, to African ubuntu philosophy, to Confucian ethics, as well as Judeo-Christian, Buddhist, Islamic, and Native American traditions -all centering love, compassion, and care.

These traditions provide instructions on how to care for oneself, how to care for and treat others, and generally how to live a 'good' life: Don't harm another (by taking their life, wife, cow, or by deception).

"Do not kill"; "speak out for those who cannot speak, for the rights of all the destitute"; "develop a mind of compassion toward all beings"; "what you do not wish for yourself, do not do to others"; "I am because we are"; "treat the earth and all that dwell thereon with respect"; "let your heart be moved with compassion for all living things"; "love thy neighbor as yourself."
Of course, morality-as-cooperation proponents could argue that 17 cooperation is in here, too -and in places it is.
But AMT predicts this; the duty network codifies cooperative norms, among many others.

While religious teachings explicitly codified care into moral principles, morality is deeply embedded in other cultural products, where moral themes arise organically and unconsciously (as evolutionary psychologists might predict of any evolved disposition).
Storytelling -from ancient myths to modern films -has both unconscious and conscious forms.

Indeed, evolutionary approaches to literature suggest that one adaptive function of stories is to expand and refine our capacity to process social information while safely exploring social conflicts and ethical dilemmas (Boyd, 2009).

text.text: Stories are seldom about cooperation or coordination, but about love, sex, compassion, loyalty, sacrifice, betrayal, duty, honor, promises, and revenge.
Fiction, Boyd argues, uniquely cultivates a moral sense.
Moral themes may be explicit and purposeful -as in fables, folk wisdom, protest art, and philosophy -aimed at shaping moral virtue and sensibility.

Kant's categorical imperative (CI) is a later and more abstract derivation of CARE: "Act in such a way that you treat humanity, whether in your own person or in that of another, never merely as a means to an end, but always at the same time as an end" (Kant, 1785 (Kant, /1998, p. 38), p. 38).

It makes care a duty.
The duty to not lie/tell the truth is likewise plausibly derived from CARE.
Deception prevents access to accurate information, potentially exposing someone to harm.

Once encoded as a rule, however, it can operate independently of its CARE origins -even when adherence itself threatens wellbeing, as in Kant's murderer-at-the-door example.
Central to many of these codes and stories are injunctions against boundary transgression -CARE formalized by Duty: justice.
While likely all ancient religious texts codified CARE into 18 duties and responsibilities, some texts also laid down laws and rights.
The ancient Babylonian Code of Hammurabi exemplifies this explicitly with 282 specific laws that aim to redress harms done (retributive justice) with punishment to the violators.

The text explicitly says that prince Hammurabi, having been given the power to do so by the gods, shall "bring about the rule of righteousness in the land, to destroy the wicked and the evil-doers; so that the strong should not harm the weak; so that [he] should rule . . . the land, to further the well-being of mankind" (King translation, emphasis added).
19   Here, justice and fairness are DN-based rules derived from CARE.
Schopenhauer recognized this.
Both "'the duties of law' [do no harm] and the 'duties of love' [helping] have their root in natural compassion. . . .
It is original and immediate, and lies in human nature itself" (1903, p. 177).

text.text: Philosopher-theologian Joseph Fletcher, whose situation ethics is taken up below, went further: "Love and justice are the same, for justice is love distributed, nothing else" (1966, p. 87).

text.text: Indeed, CARE's affiliative impulse -empathy and concern for others -is not only at the root of the DN's justice principles, it also functions as a proximate mechanism motivating (and often regulating) fairness.
As noted earlier, concern for others appears early, before rules: toddlers help others achieve their goals without prompting or reward (Warneken & Tomasello, 2009).

Perhaps AMT's closest philosophical resonance is with situation ethics.
Developed by Fletcher, its underlying structure was the Christian ethic of agape (unconditional love).
Fletcher argued 21 that moral rules ('illuminators') should generally guide behavior, but always yield when the situation warrants it.
AMT essentially naturalizes Fletcher's religious agape as our evolved CARE system, and his flexible illuminators as the DN (Fletcher, 1966).
text.formatted: AMT essentially naturalizes Fletcher's religious agape as our evolved CARE system, and his flexible illuminators as the DN <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(Fletcher, 1966)</ref>.

text.text: A related position in contemporary analytic philosophy is threshold deontology: the view that deontological duties are binding but may be overridden when sufficiently weighty moral considerations arise.
Imagine someone gives heroin to a person about to be executed.

The moral evaluation involves weighing immediate suffering (registered by CARE) against breaking the law (registered by the DN) -in this case, designed to protect long-term well-being and the broader social good.
Since the temporal context eliminates future considerations, CARE overrides the rule meant to protect future well-being.

Indeed, primal, instinctual CARE often overrides the duty network: a healthcare worker breaching confidentiality to protect safety, a parent stealing food for their hungry child, lying to protect a loved one from danger -ad infinitum.
In AMT's terms, what we experience as moral intuition -simply feeling or knowing what is right -can arise from CARE, Duty, or their interaction.
22   Eastern traditions also reveal this dual structure.
Buddhism distinguishes karuna (compassion) and metta (loving-kindness) -care-based responses to suffering -from sila, its codified rules of conduct and obligation (Harvey, 2000).
text.formatted: Buddhism distinguishes karuna (compassion) and metta (loving-kindness) -care-based responses to suffering -from sila, its codified rules of conduct and obligation <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">(Harvey, 2000)</ref>.

text.text: And, like situation ethics and threshold deontology, Buddhism (particularly Mahayana) allows overriding rule-following when it better serves the alleviation of suffering.

Hindu philosophy offers perhaps the clearest pre-theoretical expression of AMT: karuna (CARE) expresses the affective desire to reduce suffering, while dharma (Duty) represents an extensive system of role-based obligations.
In The Bhagavad Gita, Arjuna's love and compassion for his kin conflict directly with Krishna's injunction to go into battle and slay them.
Arjuna says to Krishna: "My senses are overcome by the weakness of pity, and my mind is confused about duty.
Please tell me what is better for me" (2. 7, trans. Prasad, 1988).
text.formatted: Please tell me what is better for me" (2. <ref type="bibr">7, trans. Prasad, 1988</ref>).

text.text: Fletcher's theological view may explain why situation ethics never gained substantial traction in secular moral philosophy, 21 despite its intuitive appeal.
AMT proposes that a similar structure emerges naturalistically from our evolved neurobiology.
Confucian philosophy also reveals a parallel C/D duality: ren -benevolence, empathy, and concern for others' well-being; li -norms, roles, rituals.
But li requires ren lest it be hollow (Confucius, 1998, 3.3).

text.text: Across time and cultures, the C/D moral structure has been intuited and expressed, though an extensive search (beyond the scope of this paper) would likely reveal further parallels.

Our everyday lives are filled with moral decisions which often involve weighing self-interest (proto-CARE) against rules and obligations (Duty) and care for others (CARE) -as in deciding whether to break a law, keep a promise, help a friend, betray a spouse, or tell the truth.

Moral decision-making also varies considerably across individuals, reflecting among other factors, differences in cognitive processing and norm sensitivity, as well as in affective sensitivity, regulation, and orientation.
For instance, some individuals, whether by nature, nurture, or both, are more empathic -weighted more toward others than self.
At the other end of the spectrum are those with a self-centered orientation with little or no care for others.
In AMT's terms, someone with this disposition would be operating from a One Life Matters (only) moral frame.
Moral frames can be used for any moral dilemma, real or abstract, but become particularly salient in abstract and hypothetical dilemmas, discussed below.
The CARE system responds directly to welfare in the here and now.
Seeing someone drowning, for example, may produce an immediate impulse to rush in to save them -or inhibit us from pushing someone from a footbridge, even if it saves many lives.
But what about the future?
Prospection -the capacity to mentally simulate possible futures (Suddendorf & Corballis, 2007; Seligman et al., 2013) -enables us to think about outcomes, whether they be of a moral or nonmoral kind.

text.text: In the moral realm, CARE can extend forward in time.
When deciding whether to keep a secret, for example, we may weigh our duty to honor confidentiality against the potential future harm that could come from not sharing the information.
AMT calls this projection of concern for well-being into the future CARE prospection -consequentialist reasoning.

Panel B shows how both systems can inform the valuation of lives in abstract moral dilemmas.
The same action can be motivated by CARE, Duty, or both.
For example, a parent may care for a child out of love (CARE), a sense of filial obligation (Duty), or both.
A firefighter may enter a burning building from an immediate protective impulse (CARE), professional duty (DN), or both.
When subjects wrestle with moral dilemmas, they may do so from one or more of eight moral frames (cognitive schemas), which map a space of moral orientations toward life.

In everyday 23 moral life, the particularist frame Some Lives Matter (more than others) often predominates, 24 especially its relationship-based arm where valuation may arise from CARE-based bonds or Duty-based obligations.
In abstract dilemmas, however, the absence of individuating information may favor a shift toward the universalist All Lives Matter (equally) frame, in which every life counts equally.

ALM is not confined to abstract dilemmas, however; its impartiality principle can also inform everyday judgments of fairness, such as the equal distribution of resources, the domain of the shared-resources rule (Fig. 1), from which ALM could have derived.

text.text: Some frames happen to reflect stable orientations or psychological dispositions -as in the case of One Life Matters (only) -but here, the frames are perspectives or stances one might adopt when reasoning through a particular dilemma.
Therefore, someone could be a universalist -All Lives Matter (equally) -by dint of religion, yet operate from a different frame when confronted with moral decisions.
In abstract sacrificial dilemmas, CARE's merit-based arm of Some Lives Matter (more than others) may favor saving a doctor over an anonymous bystander because of the greater good she may go on to do.
This valuation may arise intuitively, through learned associations between doctors and the well-being of others, or through CARE prospection -thinking about the lives she might save.
The duty network can produce similar consequentialist outcomes with an established rule such as a protocol prioritizing healthcare workers.
Such rules are efficient -CARE prospection codified -producing well-being benefits without case-by-case consequentialist reasoning.
The moral frame All Lives Matter (equally), however, is instantiated in the duty network by a rule: count every life equally.
The save more lives algorithm follows: five outweigh one.
The result is a consequentialist outcome reached without consequentialist reasoning.

text.text: These gedanken experiments, and the many variations that followed, have become central to moral philosophy and moral psychology, particularly in research on the apparent divide between deontological and consequentialist -and more specifically utilitarian -judgments.
In the standard switch dilemma, a trolley is barreling toward five people, but a bystander can pull a switch diverting it onto a side track where only one person stands.
Remarkably, one study that included 42 countries and 70,000 participants found that 81% of respondents would pull the switch (Awad et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Remarkably, one study that included 42 countries and 70,000 participants found that 81% of respondents would pull the switch <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Awad et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Such responses are conventionally classified as utilitarian and often understood as reflective of consequentialist reasoning -weighing outcomes to bring about the greater good.
AMT hypothesizes instead that some, perhaps many, of these respondents have shifted to the ALM frame and are running the duty network's save more lives algorithm.
If so, choosing the switch would be consequentialist in outcome but not in cognitive process.

(Which process predominates is an empirical question.) 29   Greene's dual-process theory proposes that social-emotional and cognitive processes both contribute to moral judgment and can come into conflict (Greene et al., 2001 (Greene et al., , 2004;; Greene, 2008).

text.text: He distinguishes personal dilemmas, such as footbridge, in which one directly causes serious harm to an identifiable person, from impersonal ones, such as switch, which lack one or more of these features.

For Greene, personal dilemmas elicit emotional responses that drive the deontological judgment (don't push); impersonal ones engage controlled cognition and yield the utilitarian judgment (pull the switch).
This makes intuitive sense when using the emotion/reason dichotomy.
But as AMT argues, morality should be carved at a different joint.
For AMT, the aversion to pushing in footbridge reflects the CARE system, potentially reinforced by the duty network's prohibition against harm.
In switch, the 'personal' features that strongly recruit CARE are diminished, allowing rule-based judgment to play a greater role.
One such rule is ALM's count every life equally, which yields the familiar five-over-one response.
Thus, what looks like a utilitarian response need not arise from consequentialist reasoning.

Trolley problems chiefly bear on the contrast between ALM and SLM, but other moral frames may also shape responses.
One is Life Matters (but it's not in one's control), the fatalist frame.
A respondent who declines to pull the switch may not be following a prohibition against killing, as researchers might infer, but deferring moral agency to fate, the cosmos, or God.
On this view, it is not one's place to determine who lives and who dies.
Thus, the fatalist frame offers an interpretation of inaction that differs from those ordinarily considered in trolley research.
The remaining frames may also illuminate sacrificial dilemmas and moral decision-making more broadly, but exploring their applications lies beyond the scope of this paper.
Adaptive moral theory integrates evolutionary science, neuroscience, and cognitive science to offer a new lens on our evolved moral sense, reframing enduring debates in moral philosophy.
It posits two functional moral systems in humans -the CARE system and the duty network.
The ancient CARE system is oriented toward the well-being of others; the phylogenetically newer duty network, toward rules, commitments, and obligations.
Both the CARE system and the duty network can extend beyond their evolutionary origins.
CARE reaches beyond its original relational targets (e.g., saving a stranger), the DN beyond the well-being it originally served (e.g., blunt truth where a white lie would be kinder).
Both can also extend beyond the present: CARE through prospection, the DN through commitments.
And each system's strength is also its liability: CARE's partiality can narrow into tribalism; the DN's rules can be applied harshly.
When the systems conflict, situation ethics can help recalibrate.
The inherited philosophical debates about the binaries (consequentialism/deontology and emotion/cognition) have shaped what moral psychologists ask -and what they look for in the brain.

Indeed, these framings led Greene (2008) to identify four empirical possibilities by crossing the two binaries -as if these were the only axes available -roughly associating cognition with consequentialist judgments and emotional responses with deontological judgments.

text.text: AMT argues that this framing carves the moral mind and brain at the wrong joints.
A division that better reflects our moral sense is functional: the CARE system and the duty network.
Cognition and emotion are necessary for a moral sense, but they are not its operating systems.
CARE is affective-motivational but recruits cognition, as in prospection; the duty network is rule-based, but its violation detection elicits emotions.
For AMT, although we may at times weigh well-being outcomes against duties, the two do not have parallel bases in the brain.
Capacities central to deontology have a neural basis in the duty network, whereas consequentialist reasoning is a cognitive operation recruited by the CARE system (CARE prospection).
Consequentialist outcomes need not involve consequentialist 30 reasoning: duty network rules can produce them as well.
AMT is also empirically testable.

When Curry and colleagues conducted a large neuroimaging study, they found no associations between his seven moral domains and regional grey matter volume, leading them to call for theory-driven, a priori predictions -and functional rather than structural measures (Wilkinson et al., 2024).

text.text: AMT offers exactly such predictions.
It also advances a set of hypotheses and opens new lines of inquiry across philosophy, neuroscience, cognitive science, and psychology.
Among them: 1.
Care, not cooperation, is foundational and fundamental to morality.
The duty network provides a fundamental neural basis for the human capacity to represent and apply moral duties and obligations -capacities central to deontology.
Compressed into duty network rules, that concern can yield consequentialist outcomes without consequentialist reasoning.

Just as consequentialist reasoning, on AMT's account, involves general cognitive capacities recruited by the CARE system for 30 prospection, what we call "moral cognition" may be better understood as general cognitive capacities engaged by the CARE system and duty network rather than a faculty in its own right.
A fuller treatment awaits future work.
